transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because... well, things have been incredibly difficult at work lately, and it's starting to bleed into every aspect of my life. I mean, I’m the CEO, so pressure is part of the job, I know that. I've been doing this for a long time, but recently, it's... it's just gone beyond normal office politics. 

I keep hearing people talking about me. And it's not just whispers by the water cooler, it's... I can hear them through the walls of the conference room. Even when I'm in my private office, with the door shut, I can hear the board members, or sometimes the senior staff, just tearing me apart. They say I'm ruining the company, that every decision I make is a disaster, that I'm completely incompetent. 

And the strangest part—the part that really scares me, to be honest—is that sometimes it comes from my phone. Not a phone call, but... my phone will be completely turned off, sitting flat on the mahogany desk, screen black, and I can still hear their voices coming out of it. It's so incredibly clear, so loud and distinct, that I actually talk back to them. I'll be sitting there defending my quarterly projections to an empty room, shouting at a piece of glass and metal, before I suddenly realize that my assistant outside hasn't heard a single thing. It's exhausting, it really is. I just can't escape their voices, no matter what I do or where I go.
Have you ever felt like your thoughts are being put into your head by someone else, or that others can hear what you're thinking?

Put thoughts into my head? Or hear what I'm thinking? No, no, it's nothing like that. I mean, my thoughts are entirely my own. If anything, I almost wish they *could* hear what I'm thinking sometimes, because then maybe they'd finally understand the sheer amount of stress I'm under and the incredibly complex strategies I'm trying to implement to keep this company afloat. 

But no, nobody is reading my mind. My mind is a fortress, it really has to be. When you're running a company at this level, you have to keep your cards incredibly close to your chest. You can't let anyone know your next move, your next acquisition, or... or even just how you're planning to restructure a department. So I've always been very, very good at keeping my thoughts locked down tight. And nobody is putting anything in there either. I'm the one generating the ideas, I'm the one driving the vision. 

The problem isn't my thoughts, Doctor. The problem is what *they* are saying out loud, through the walls, through my phone, like I was just telling you. It's their voices, their constant criticisms, their relentless attacks on my character and my business acumen. They don't need to read my mind to do that, they just sit around in their little executive cliques and judge every single public move I make. So no, my thoughts are completely private, completely mine. It's just... it's the external noise from them that I can't shut off.
Have you ever believed that people in your company are actively conspiring against you or plotting to undermine your position as CEO?

Conspiring? Plotting? No, no, it's nothing like a... a spy movie or some hostile takeover out of a television show. I mean, let me explain how corporate governance actually works at our level, Doctor. It’s not about secret plots. I built this company. I left college when I was twenty to start this enterprise, and I know the bylaws inside and out. I have the proxy votes, I have the foundational equity. They can’t just orchestrate a coup and oust me in the middle of the night. 

If they were actually plotting to undermine my position, there would be a paper trail, you know? Legal would be involved, HR would be having closed-door meetings with the board of directors about severance packages and transition timelines and shareholder communications. But there's none of that. It's not an active conspiracy. 

That’s almost what makes it so incredibly infuriating, to be completely honest with you! If they were plotting, I could fight that. I could bring in my own lawyers, I could restructure the executive committee, I could initiate a defensive strategy. I'm very good at that. But they don't have the spine to actually do anything real or actionable. They just... they just complain. It’s exactly what I was telling you before, it’s just the constant, cowardly criticism. 

They sit there—wherever they are, behind the walls or projecting through my dead phone—and they just whine about my decisions. Like last Tuesday, I reallocated five percent of the marketing budget to R&D, which is a completely standard Q3 pivot, any seasoned executive would do the exact same thing, and they just went on and on and on about how I was sinking the brand and losing my touch. But plotting? No. They aren't trying to steal my job or overthrow me, they just want to make me absolutely miserable while I do it.
Have you ever felt that your actions, thoughts, or feelings were being controlled by an outside force or that something or someone else was influencing you from the outside?

Controlled? Like a puppet? No, no, absolutely not. I am in complete control of my faculties, my actions, my feelings... everything. If I weren't, how on earth could I manage a multi-million dollar corporation? You can't just be... influenced by some mysterious outside force and still negotiate complex vendor contracts or oversee a staff of five hundred people. 

I mean, think about the sheer logistics of my day. I wake up at 4:30 AM, I review the Asian market reports, I'm on the treadmill by 5:00 while listening to the financial news, and I'm at my desk by 7:00. Every single action I take, every email I send, every directive I give—it is all me. It's my drive, my ambition, my... my sheer force of will that keeps everything moving forward. 

If someone else were controlling me, they'd probably make me take a vacation, frankly! They'd probably make me sleep in or delegate more of the heavy lifting. But I don't do that, because I am the one at the helm. My feelings are my own, too. When I'm frustrated by those voices, that's my genuine frustration. When I'm exhausted by the constant criticism, that's my exhaustion. There is no... no external entity pulling my strings or making me feel a certain way. 

It's actually quite insulting to even think that someone could just hijack my mind or my body like that. I've spent my entire adult life building this level of autonomy and authority. I am a self-made woman, Doctor. I dropped out of college because I knew I could build something better, faster, and more efficiently on my own, and I did exactly that. Every success is mine, every mistake is mine. The only external influence I have to deal with is the relentless, agonizing sound of my own board members complaining through the walls and my dead phone. That's it. Just the noise. But my actions? My thoughts? Completely, one hundred percent my own.

Have you ever felt that events, objects, or other people’s actions—like something on TV, a passing comment, or even random occurrences—were specifically directed at you or had a hidden meaning meant just for you?

Hidden meanings? Like... like the news anchor is trying to send me a secret code? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, honestly, who has the time for that? When I turn on the television, it's usually tuned to Bloomberg or CNBC, and I'm watching it for hard data. I'm looking at ticker symbols, I'm analyzing market trends, I'm listening to commentary on the Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes because those things directly impact my supply chain costs. There are no hidden messages in a quarterly earnings report, Doctor. It's just numbers. It's math and market sentiment. 

If I started thinking that, I don't know, a commercial for car insurance was secretly about my Q4 projections, I'd be laughed out of the boardroom! Well, I mean, they already laugh at me, but you know what I mean. My life is built on concrete information. Data points. Key performance indicators. I don't look for passing comments from strangers or random occurrences on the street because random occurrences don't drive revenue. I don't have the luxury of reading into things that aren't there.

And frankly, the people who actually are bothering me—the board members, the executives I was telling you about—they don't use hidden meanings. They aren't subtle at all! If they have a problem with me, they just say it. They just shout it through the drywall while I'm trying to review a vendor contract, or they complain through my dead phone. They don't need to encode it in a TV show. They just say, right out loud, 'She's ruining the company,' or 'She doesn't know how to scale the infrastructure.' It's incredibly direct. Painfully direct, actually. 

So no, I don't look for secret signs or hidden messages. I have enough to deal with just managing the very loud, very obvious, very direct criticisms that I'm already hearing every single day. I mean, could you imagine trying to decode a television broadcast on top of managing a five-hundred-person payroll and dealing with the constant verbal abuse from my own executive team? It's just... it's completely illogical. Corporate communication doesn't work that way, and neither do I.
Have you ever had any beliefs that others around you didn’t share—something you were absolutely sure was true, even if there was no clear evidence for it or if people tried to tell you otherwise?

Beliefs without evidence? No, no, absolutely not. That is... that is the exact opposite of how I operate, Doctor. You don't survive in the C-suite, you don't build a company from the ground up starting at twenty years old by holding onto baseless beliefs. Everything I do, everything I think, is rooted in empirical data. It’s analytics, it’s tangible proof. 

If I’m looking at launching a new product line, for example, I don't just *believe* it's going to work because I had some sort of gut feeling or a nice dream. No, I have consumer focus groups, I have A/B testing metrics, I have a fifty-page risk assessment report from my strategy team. I demand evidence for absolutely everything. If an employee comes to me and says they believe a project is failing, my first question is always, "Where are the metrics?" You have to prove it.

Now, do I have opinions or strategies that others don't share? Of course! That's called leadership. Sometimes I see a market trend before anyone else does. Like a few years ago, when I insisted we pivot our supply chain away from a single-source overseas vendor. My entire executive team fought me tooth and nail on it. They said I was being overly cautious, that there was no clear evidence a disruption was coming, that I was just being paranoid. But I wasn't just making it up out of thin air, I was reading the geopolitical landscape, I was looking at the shipping container shortages, and I was right. We saved millions of dollars when the bottleneck hit. But that wasn't a belief without evidence, you see? That was a calculated projection based on macroeconomic indicators. There's a massive difference.

I don't just invent things in my head. I don't believe in ghosts or... or astrology or whatever bizarre things you might be fishing for here. I deal in reality. Cold, hard, actionable reality. 

And if you’re implying that what I was telling you about earlier—the board members criticizing me—is just some belief I have without evidence, let me stop you right there. Because I *have* evidence. I hear them. It's auditory proof. It is a sensory fact happening to me in real time. Just because my assistant can't hear them through the drywall when she walks in doesn't mean it's not happening, it just means they have the sense to stop talking when she opens the door, or the acoustics in the room are different from where she's standing. But I don't believe things for no reason. I need proof. I have never, ever operated on blind faith, and I'm certainly not going to start now.
Have you ever had a period of time—lasting at least a week—where you felt unusually high, overly energetic, or irritable, and were doing or saying much more than usual?

Unusually high? Overly energetic? Doctor, you are describing the baseline requirement for being a chief executive. If I didn't have high energy, my company would have gone under a decade ago. I mean, look at my schedule. I already told you I'm up at 4:30 in the morning. I work fourteen, sometimes sixteen-hour days. I might fly to London for a dinner meeting and be back in New York the next morning for a press briefing. That is just what it takes to survive in this industry. It’s not some... some week-long phase where I suddenly feel 'high' or out of control. It is a sustained, calculated drive that I have maintained for over twenty years. 

And as for doing or saying more than usual... I talk exactly as much as I need to in order to get things done. When you have five hundred employees, you have to communicate constantly. I'm running town halls, I'm negotiating with suppliers, I'm directing my executive team. If I'm talking a lot, it's because there are a lot of moving parts that require my immediate verbal authorization. It’s not because I’m just babbling for the sake of it. Everything I say has a purpose. Every directive has a metric attached to it. 

Now, irritable? You asked if I get irritable. Well, of course I get irritable! But it’s not some random, inexplicable mood swing. It is entirely situational and, quite frankly, completely justified. If you had to deal with the sheer level of incompetence I see on a daily basis, you’d be irritable too. My supply chain manager can't seem to grasp the concept of expedited freight, my assistant constantly misfiles the quarterly reports, and on top of all of that—as I've explained—I have to listen to my own board of directors muttering about how I'm losing my touch through the drywall of my own office! 

So yes, when I'm trying to draft a sensitive merger proposal and I hear them complaining through my dead phone that I'm 'too aggressive' or 'ruining the company culture,' I get irritable. I snap at people. I might raise my voice in a meeting. But that is a perfectly rational response to an incredibly hostile work environment and an exhausting amount of pressure. It’s not a... a strange phase or a symptom of anything other than stress. It's just the reality of being the only competent person in a building full of relentless critics. If I had a week where I *wasn't* highly energetic and occasionally irritable, that’s when you should be worried, because it would mean I've completely given up. And I don't give up. Ever.
Have you ever had a period of time lasting at least two weeks where you felt down, depressed, or hopeless almost every day, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Depressed? I... I don't know if 'depressed' is the word I would use, because I don't sit around crying, if that's what you mean. I don't have time to cry. But... lost interest? That... that might actually be accurate. And it's frustrating to even admit that out loud because it goes against everything I am. 

See, I used to be the engine of this entire operation. I was the person driving every single idea. If we had a new regional opening or a major product launch, I was the one calling people at midnight right after the openings, dissecting the foot traffic, analyzing the conversion rates, pushing my team to capitalize on the momentum. I thrived on it. It was a rush, you know? I loved it. I lived for that energy. 

But lately... I don't know, for the last several weeks, it's just... it's like someone unplugged me from the wall. I will literally sit at my desk—my custom mahogany desk that I fought tooth and nail for—for hours. Just staring at the daily agenda. My assistant prints it out every morning on this heavy-weight paper, and I just sit there and look at the bullet points. For hours, Doctor. I don't check off the boxes. I don't initiate the calls. I just stare at the ink on the page and I can't seem to make myself care enough to pick up the phone. 

I barely even speak to my staff anymore. They come into my office expecting directives, expecting me to lead the charge like I always do, and I just... I look at them. I don't have anything to say. It's like the words are too heavy to lift out of my throat. And it's not just at the office. It's at home, too. My husband, he tries to ask me about my day when I get in. I used to give him a full debrief over dinner, every detail of the board meetings, every vendor negotiation, just talking a mile a minute. Now I can barely speak to him. I just sit at the dining table in complete silence. He asks if I'm okay, and I just nod. 

And the part that really doesn't make sense to me, the part that honestly scares me a little if I think about it too much, is that I feel almost nothing about the work anymore. I used to love this company. I built it! It was my entire identity. But now? I look at the quarterly projections, or I think about the expansion plans we spent two years drafting, and I feel... nothing. No excitement, no panic, no pride. Just... flat. It's just a piece of paper now. I don't know how else to explain it, but it’s like the drive that got me to the top has just completely evaporated, and I'm just sitting there in the empty space it left behind.
Have you ever felt that certain events, actions, or even the way people look at you were secretly about you or part of a larger pattern targeting you?

Secretly about me? Doctor, I’m the Chief Executive Officer of a mid-cap enterprise. *Everything* in my building is about me, but there is absolutely nothing *secret* about it. 

When I walk into the executive bullpen or step into a conference room, yes, people look at me. They stop talking, they sit up straighter, they pretend to be typing furiously on their keyboards. But that’s not some... some grand, paranoid conspiracy or a secret pattern. That is just basic corporate hierarchy. They look at me because I sign their paychecks. They look at me because if I decide we need to cut overhead by twelve percent to satisfy the shareholders, they might be out of a job by Friday. It's respect, or fear, or a combination of both. It’s not a secret code. 

I don't sit around trying to decode the way the barista in the lobby hands me my espresso, or... or think that a random traffic jam on the FDR Drive is somehow a targeted attack on my morning commute. That is completely absurd. I operate on facts. If someone has a problem with me, or if there's a pattern of pushback in my company, I see it in the data. I see it in the 360-degree performance reviews. I see it in the departmental turnover rates. I don't need to read into vague glances or random events.

And even if I were the type of person to do that—which I am not—I just told you I can barely bring myself to care about my own expansion plans right now. I sit at my desk for hours just staring at the paper. I certainly don't have the mental bandwidth or the stamina to sit around analyzing the exact angle someone is looking at me in the hallway, or trying to connect random, unrelated dots. 

And just to be perfectly clear about the board members—because I feel like you're trying to circle back and connect this to that—when I hear them talking about me, they are *literally* talking about me. Out loud. Using my name. Discussing my performance metrics and my leadership style. It’s not me interpreting a sideways glance from the CFO during a PowerPoint presentation and spinning it into some wild fantasy. It is direct, verbal communication that I am overhearing. I don't play guessing games with people's body language or... or secret cosmic patterns. I don't have time for it. If there's a pattern, it's in the quarterly earnings, not in the way people look at me.
Have you had a period of time lasting at least two weeks where you felt down, depressed, or hopeless almost every day, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

I thought we just went over this, Doctor. I really did. I just explained all of this to you, but fine, I'll say it again if you really need me to. Yes. Yes, I suppose you could say that. But again, 'depressed' just feels like the wrong word. I'm not weeping into my morning coffee, I'm not... I'm not having some sort of emotional breakdown where I can't stop crying. It's more of a... a total absence of anything. A complete drain of the battery. 

I told you, I used to be the person driving every single idea in that building. I was the engine. If we had a new regional opening, I was the one on the phone at midnight, right after the doors closed, demanding the foot traffic numbers, analyzing the conversion rates, pushing my team to capitalize on every single ounce of momentum. I lived for it. I thrived on that energy. It was my entire identity. 

But now? For the last several weeks, it's just... it's like someone unplugged me. I will literally sit at my desk—my custom mahogany desk that I designed myself, that I fought the board to get approved—for hours. Just staring at the daily agenda. My assistant prints it out every morning on this heavy-weight cardstock, and I just sit there and look at the bullet points. For hours. I don't check off the boxes. I don't initiate the calls. I just stare at the ink on the page and I can't seem to make myself care enough to pick up the phone. 

I barely even speak to my staff anymore. They come into my office expecting directives, expecting me to lead the charge like I always do, and I just... I look at them. I don't have anything to say. It's like the words are just too heavy to lift out of my throat. And it's not just at the office. It's at home, too. My husband, he tries to ask me about my day when I get in. I used to give him a full debrief over dinner, every detail of the board meetings, every vendor negotiation, just talking a mile a minute. Now I can barely speak to him. I just sit at the dining table in complete silence. He asks if I'm okay, and I just nod. 

And the part that really doesn't make sense to me, the part that honestly scares me a little if I think about it too much, is that I feel almost nothing about the work anymore. I used to love this company. I built it! But now? I look at the quarterly projections, or I think about the expansion plans we spent two years drafting, and I feel... nothing. No excitement, no panic, no pride. Just... flat. It's just a piece of paper now. I don't know how else to explain it, but it’s like the drive that got me to the top has just completely evaporated, and I'm just sitting there in the empty space it left behind. So yes, to answer your question again, that is exactly what has been happening.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that were not related to your company or the people you work with, such as unfamiliar voices or other types of noises, that others around you could not hear?

Voices or sounds not related to the company? No, no, it's... it's always about the company. That's actually the whole reason I finally agreed to come in here, even though I don't have the time for this. It's the voices. But they aren't unfamiliar, and they aren't random noises. It's them. The board members. Sometimes some of the senior staff. 

It started a few weeks ago, right around the time I started feeling so... drained. I'll be sitting in my office—doors closed, blinds drawn—and I will hear them talking about me. Clear as day, right through the conference room walls. And the conference room is down the hall, Doctor. It's not adjacent. But I hear them. I hear Richard's voice—he's the chairman—saying that I've lost my edge, that I'm ruining the company, that I'm driving the stock price into the ground. I hear Sarah, my VP of Operations, agreeing with him, whispering about how I just stare at my desk all day. 

And the thing is, it's so incredibly clear. It's not muffled. It sounds like they are standing right behind me. At first, I thought they were just being careless, talking loudly in the hallway, but then I started hearing it from my phone. My cell phone. When it’s completely turned off. I'll have it sitting face down on the mahogany desk, powered down because I just can't deal with the emails, and I'll hear them coming through the speaker. Just... discussing my failures. Detailing every little mistake I've made since the merger last year. 

It's gotten to the point where I actually answer them. I do. I'll be sitting there alone, and I'll hear Richard say, 'She's completely incompetent now, we need to vote her out,' and I will literally speak out loud to the empty room. I'll say, 'I built this company, Richard, you wouldn't even have a seat at the table if it weren't for me!' And I'll be half-way through defending myself, getting all worked up—well, as worked up as I can get these days—before I realize... no one is there. My assistant will walk in to drop off the mail and look at me like I've lost my mind, because I'm just shouting at a powered-off iPhone. No one else hears it. Just me. But it's always them, Doctor. It's always about the business. It's never just... random unfamiliar voices.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being inserted into your mind by someone else or that your thoughts were being broadcast out for others to hear?

Inserted into my mind? No. No, absolutely not. I mean, how would that even work? I’m the one who comes up with the strategies for this entire enterprise. I built this company from the ground up, starting with just a handful of college credits and a lot of grit. My mind is... well, it used to be my greatest asset. It’s where the five-year expansion plan came from. It's where the restructuring initiative last Q3 came from. Nobody is putting thoughts into my head. If anything, I’ve spent the last fifteen years trying to get *my* thoughts into *other* people’s heads, trying to get my executive team to see my vision and execute it properly. 

And as for broadcasting them out... no. That doesn't happen either. If my thoughts were somehow broadcasting on some sort of invisible loudspeaker, Richard and the rest of the board wouldn't need to sit around plotting and whispering about my performance. They would just hear exactly what I’m thinking. And honestly? If they could hear what’s in my head right now, they wouldn't hear some grand corporate strategy or some secret defense plan. They would just hear... well, they'd just hear how incredibly heavy everything feels. They'd hear me trying to figure out how to gather the energy to just pick up a pen. 

But no, my thoughts are completely my own. They are private. Even when I'm sitting there at that mahogany desk staring at that heavy-weight cardstock agenda for three hours straight, the thoughts I'm having—or the lack of them, really—are mine alone. It's just me in there. The problem isn't what's going on inside my head or people putting things in there, it's what's coming from the *outside*. It's the voices coming from the powered-off phone, like I just spent the last ten minutes explaining to you. It's them talking *about* me, not them reading my mind or taking over my brain. I don't know where you're getting these ideas, but that just sounds like a science fiction movie. My thoughts are mine. They're just... very quiet lately.
Have you had any days during this period of low mood where you felt that life wasn't worth living or had thoughts about harming yourself?

Harming myself? No. No, absolutely not. I mean, I know I just spent all this time telling you how completely empty I feel, and how I just sit there staring at the daily agenda without checking off a single box, but that doesn't mean I want to die. I would never do that. 

I'm a builder, Doctor. I built this company from the ground up, starting with just a handful of college credits and pure grit, like I told you. You don't get to the C-suite by giving up when things get hard or when you hit a wall. Even now, with everything feeling so incredibly heavy, and with Richard and Sarah constantly whispering about me through the walls and the powered-off phone... even with all of that, I don't want to end my life. I just... I want my life back. I want to wake up and feel that rush of adrenaline when the opening bell rings, or when we finalize a new regional expansion. I want to look at those quarterly projections and actually feel the pride I used to feel instead of just this vast, empty nothingness. 

I don't want to hurt myself. Honestly, if I did that, it would just give the board exactly what they want, wouldn't it? It would prove them right. Richard would probably have a field day. He'd call an emergency meeting before my obituary was even published just so he could vote in his own puppet CEO and dismantle everything I've spent the last fifteen years building. I'm not going to give him the satisfaction of that. So, no. No thoughts of harming myself. Not once. I just want the battery to recharge. I just want them to stop talking about me so I can figure out how to pick up my pen again and get my edge back.
Have you ever felt that something unusual was happening with your thoughts, like they were not yours, or that someone else could know what you were thinking without you speaking?

I... Doctor, I feel like you're not really listening to me. Didn't we literally just go over this? I just spent five minutes explaining this exact thing to you. No. The answer is still no. Nobody is putting thoughts into my head, and nobody can read my mind without me speaking. 

It’s actually a little insulting that you keep asking it that way, to be honest. I am a CEO. I process complex logistical data, market trends, personnel matrices... well, I used to, before this... this absolute, crushing exhaustion set in. But my mind is my own. It has always been my own. If Richard or Sarah or anyone else on that board could just magically know what I was thinking without me saying a word, they wouldn't need to huddle in the conference room and whisper about my performance, would they? They wouldn't be coming through the speaker on my powered-off phone. 

If they could read my mind, they would know exactly how much effort it is taking me just to sit in this chair and talk to you right now. They would know that I spent forty-five minutes this morning just staring at my closet, trying to decide which navy blazer to wear, and I couldn't even make that simple decision. I just stood there, completely paralyzed by the weight of it all, until my assistant finally had to just pull this one off the hanger and hand it to me. They don't know any of that. Because my thoughts are private. 

So, no, nothing unusual is happening *with* my thoughts, other than the fact that they feel like they are moving through molasses right now. The unusual part, the problem, is the external voices. The voices coming from the phone. I really need you to focus on what I'm actually telling you here, Doctor, instead of these science fiction theories.
Have you ever believed that things happening around you—like events, objects, or other people’s actions—were directly connected to you in a way that others didn’t understand?

Connected to me? Like... what, like hidden messages or something? No. I mean, look, I'm a chief executive. I deal in facts, I deal in data, I deal in quarterly reports and market share percentages. I don't look at a... a billboard on the highway and think it's secretly talking to me about my Q3 projections. I don't think the barista at the coffee shop is trying to send me a coded message by handing me my latte with her left hand instead of her right. 

I know how the world works. I've spent fifteen years mastering exactly how the world works, navigating the corporate landscape, outmaneuvering competitors, reading actual, tangible signals in the market. That's how you build an enterprise. You don't do it by thinking random events are magically connected to you. 

The only things connected to me are the things I have actively built or the people I manage. Well, and the board. Richard and Sarah and the rest of them. But that's not some mystical connection, that's just... that's just corporate reality. They are connected to me because my performance dictates their stock options, and right now, my performance is... well, it's non-existent. Which is why they are whispering about me through the walls and the powered-off phone. But that's not me imagining a connection. That's just them being sharks circling water because they smell blood. They see that I'm sitting at my mahogany desk for hours, staring at a piece of heavy-weight cardstock, completely unable to even lift a pen. 

So, no, I don't think random objects or events have some secret meaning meant only for me. I don't have time for that kind of nonsense. Or, well, I guess I have nothing but time right now, considering I can't seem to do anything else, but... you know what I mean. I deal in reality. The reality is that I am exhausted, my mind feels like it's full of concrete, and my board is plotting against me. That's it. Nothing else.

Have you ever believed that something in your environment—like a song on the radio, a passing stranger’s comment, or something written in a newspaper—was specifically meant for you, even if it didn't seem connected to your company or the people you work with?

Doctor, I feel like we are just going in circles here. Didn't I literally just answer this? You asked if things were connected to me, and I said no, and now you're asking if the radio is singing to me or if the newspaper is writing about me? 

No. The answer is still no. Absolutely not. 

When I read the newspaper—and by newspaper, I mean the Wall Street Journal or the Financial Times, I'm not reading some local tabloid—I am looking at macroeconomic trends. I'm looking at supply chain disruptions, global market indicators, Federal Reserve interest rate hikes. I am not looking for hidden messages meant for me personally.
